> > nspec <- dim(Ycd)[3]
> >
> > const <- list(year=c(rep(1,14),rep(2,14)), Year=as.vector(scale(c(rep(1,14),rep(2,14)))), nyear=nyear, nsite=nsite, ncar=nsite/2, nrep=nrep, nspec=nspec,

> >

> >   beta0 = matrix(rnorm(dim(Ycd)[3]*nyear),
> >                  nrow = dim(Ycd)[3], ncol = nyear),                                              # starting value for abundance intercept (spp and year specific)

> > > I think the foldCVstandardError uses a batch means method (or moving block bootstrap) to estimate the Monte Carlo error in the cross-validation prediction error for each fold.  Getting these error estimates is not necessary to make use of cross validation, but it can be informative.  I agree it is suspicious for it to be zero in every fold (or any fold).  That might reflect that the MCMC for each fold is not mixing.  Can you try using returnSamples = TRUE to check on whether the samples are mixing? > > > > After accounting for spatial autocorrelation in various community N-mixture models estimated, I am currently using runCrossValidate( ) to conduct k-fold cross-validation to select between candidate models. As Hooten and Hobbs (2015) note, WAIC is not recommended for use in model selection when considering models that incorporate correlated error structures (e.g., spatial [conditional autoregressive] terms); hence, I am using cross-validation with a loss function, instead.
> > > >

> > > > {

> > > > commNmix_MCMCconfiguration <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)

> > > >                                    k = 5, nBootReps = 1000,
> > > >                                    foldFunction = commNmix_FoldFunction,
> > > >                                    lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
> > > >                                    MCMCcontrol = list(niter = 12500,

> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > After successful compilation, runCrossValidate( ) returns the following:

> > > > I am curious as to how/why the CV standard errors are each estimated to be 0. Could this be related to (a) my use of cross-validation on a community N-mixture model, (b) missing information in my fold/loss function(s), (c) a bug in the source code for runCrossValidate( ), or (d) something else?

Steve, I'm sorry for the delay on this, but we've got a fix for the problem you experienced in the MCMC, and it will appear in our upcoming release, within the next week or so.  Thanks for your patience.

On Fri, Sep 4, 2020 at 8:26 AM 'Steve' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> thank you Daniel for the coherent answer, much appreciated...
> Steve
>
> On Thursday, 3 September 2020 at 21:34:11 UTC+2 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> > Indeed, most unfortunately this comes down to an issue with R, and "partial matching" of list names.  The problem can be summarized by the following simplified example of the same problem:
> >
> > myList <- list(longName = 5)
> > myList$longName  ## returns 5, which is correct
> > myList$long      ## also returns 5, which is not really correct....
> >
> > In your case, the control list element that you're providing "pfOptimizeNparticles = TRUE" is unfortunately being "partially matched" by extraction of the alternate control list element named "pf", by the code "control$pf", and hence the RW_PF_block is using TRUE for the "pf" control list element, and also using TRUE for "pfOptimizeNparticles" element (as was intended).  This isn't an error in the sampler, per se, but rather a problem in how NIMBLE's MCMC samplers process control list elements - in particular those which "partially match" the names of other control list elements.
> >
> > In short - this is a problem on our end.  And it will be addressed.
> >
> > In the meantime, a workaround is provided below, where I also provide the default value (NULL) for the "pf" control list element, and now it should work fine for you.
> >
> > Thanks for raising this.
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> > ttrTimeConf$addSampler(target = c('parset','m','sdo', 'sdp','sdb','zstart'),
> >                        type = 'RW_PF_block',
> >                        control = list(
> >                            propCov = diag(dd),
> >                            adaptScaleOnly = FALSE,
> >                            latents = "z",
> >                            pf = NULL,       ## this line is new
> >                            pfOptimizeNparticles = TRUE))
> >
> >
> >
> > On Thu, Sep 3, 2020 at 3:11 PM 'Steve' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > > I am new to nimble, so I suspect that I just doing something wrong, but I cannot spot the problem. Hopefully it is so obvious that its easily spotted by more experienced users.
> > >
> > > In brief, I setup a model and it runs fine with nimbleMCMC using the default samplers. Because this is a state space model I would like to use RW_PF_block. But when I do this I get Error: $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors.
> > >
> > > My model comes with quite a bit of baggage. I have made a portable version of the problem. This mimics the structure that I have used and reproduces the error. The error message is rather generic though and does not help me.
> > >
> > > pasted below is a portable version of the problem/mistake.
> > >
> > > rm(list=ls())
> > > library(nimble)
> > >
> > > # make some data
> > > n <- 100 # number of data points
> > > t <- seq(0,4*pi,,100)
> > > a <- 3
> > > b <- 2
> > > amp <- 2
> > > vi <- a*sin(b*t)+rnorm(n)*amp
> > > TAIR <- a*sin(b*t)+rnorm(n)*amp
> > >
> > > input.data = list(TAIR = TAIR)
> > > input.data$lo <- rep(0,7)
> > > input.data$up <- rep(1,7)
> > > input.data$mu <- input.data$up - input.data$lo
> > > input.data$steps <- n
> > >
> > > inits.data = list(parset=runif(2,0,1))
> > > inits.data$sdb <- 0.01
> > > inits.data$sdp <- 0.01
> > > inits.data$sdo <- 0.01
> > > inits.data$m <- 1.0
> > > inits.data$zstart <- 0.5
> > >
> > > resp.data <- list(vi = vi)
> > >
> > > ttrTimeNimble <- nimbleCode({
> > >
> > >     for(i in 1: 2) {
> > >      parset[i] ~ T( dnorm( mu[i], sdb), lo[i], up[i] )
> > >      }
> > >
> > >      sdp ~ dunif(lo[3], up[3])       # process error
> > >      sdo ~ dunif(lo[4], up[4])       # observation error
> > >      sdb ~ dunif(lo[6], up[6])
> > >      zstart ~ T( dnorm(mu[5],sd=sdp),lo[5], up[5])
> > >      m ~ T(dnorm(mu[7],sd=0.5),lo[7],)
> > >
> > >      z[1] <- zstart

Hi Perry et al.,

Perhaps it's not the right time just yet, but today, I happened to see that the former bug(s) in runCrossValidate( ) had recently been resolved, as was noted on the GitHub page.

After attempting to install the package using:

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

I get the following installation error:
The R package directory has not been created yet

-Perry

> > > > > >

> > > > > >   }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   MSE <- SSE / dataLength
> > > > > >   RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
> > > > > >   return(RMSE)
> > > > > > }

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I don't recall if this has come up before, so I'm not sure if this is a bug or a known limitation.

I want to write a nimble function to use within BUGS code at a deterministic node. This function will have as input some very large vectors of integers, so I would like to use integer(1) to save RAM. But the compiler fails unless I convert to double(1).   However, the original function does compile by itself (i.e. without the BUGS model). So it appears that the processing of the BUGS model is insisting integer vectors are double.

Attached is a stripped down example, including a copy-paste of the compiler error message.

Best regards
David

messages.subject: User-defined distribution problem with extreme value analysis
messages.subject_clean: User-defined distribution problem with extreme value analysis
messages.body_plain:
I have a problem defining a distribution that depends on an integer parameter that is itself variable.

I am trying to model extreme values of a set of scalar observations.  Conventionally such modelling is often done by fitting the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution to those observations that exceed some fixed high level, u, that has been chosen by the analyst. But I do not want to choose u, but rather treat u as a variable to be examined as an output of the model and whose uncertainty is taken into account in the model's uncertainty about the extreme values.

A method is described in Tancredi et al., Extremes(2006) in which all observations are taken as data, u is a variable below which the probability density of the observations are modelled as a step function with weights, (w_1,...,w_k)at an unknown number, k, of steps (a_1, ...,a_k). Above u, the density of the observations is modelled as GEV, as in the conventional approach.

I want to define a distribution that takes the factorised form:
pi(k, w, a, u, mu, psi, xi) = pi(k) pi(w, a, u | k) pi(mu, psi, xi)
where the first two factors on the right hand side relate to observations < u, and the third factor is the GEV that applies only to observations >=u.

My problem is defining in Nimble terms the distribution pi(w, a, u | k) = pi(a | k, u) pi(w|k, a, u).

For a given value of k it is easy but if k is a variable I am stuck.

I should be most grateful for any help. I have deliberately tried to keep excessive detail out of this question, if anyone needs more detail, just ask.

Many thanks

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremy,

I've done some work with extreme value analysis so have an interest in this apart from my NIMBLE work.

So I think the issue you are referring to is that the length of 'a' and 'w' will vary during the model fitting, right? You could have that length be some upper bound on 'k' and ignore some of the elements of 'a' and 'w' when 'k' is smaller than that upper bound. The problem will be that the MCMC for those unused elements of 'a' and 'w' will probably wander off without an informative prior on the elements of 'a'. But perhaps you would be ok with informative priors.

We do have a basic reversible jump sampler for variable selection in regression style problems. You might be able to modify that code for this situation - we could give some pointers if you decide to try it. Please see the code in MCMC_RJ.R in our source code.

Or you might take the kludgey approach of fitting completely separate models for a few values of k and doing model selection or model averaging.

-chris

David, thanks for the error report.

The function "extractControlElement" is a recent addition to the package.  This function should be exported when you load nimble.  Can you first just check whether:

library(nimble)
extractControlElement

is able to locate the function "extractControlElement" ?  It should, after the package is loaded, but perhaps something is going awry as a result of using pacman::p_load() ?

Another thing - did you change the "name" field of your new sampler, "sampler_RW_llFunction_block_custom", which usually is about the 2nd or 3rd line of the sampler declaration, to match the name of your new sampler, specifically, as:
...
name = 'sampler_RW_llFunction_block_custom',
...

? I'm not sure this would make the difference, but I thought I'd mention it.

Finally, I've created my own example, mimicking what (I believe) you're trying to do - see below.  It seems to work fine for me.

I hope we can figure this out without delay.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: could not find function "extractControlElement"
messages.subject_clean: could not find function "extractControlElement"
messages.body_plain:
Aha, yes, you're using version 0.9.1 of nimble, the most recent release which is on CRAN, and I'm assuming you installed it from CRAN. This change to the MCMC wasn't in that release, and hence the function "extractControlElement" isn't there (in the version of nimble you're using) at all.  Furthermore, I'm guessing you copied the source code for the "RW_llFunction_block" sampler from GitHub, from the development (the default) branch, which has this change to the MCMC.  So the version of NIMBLE you're using isn't compatible with the sample source code you copied.  So you have a bunch of easy options:

(1) Install the development version of nimble, from GitHub... code below.  Then your sampler should work fine (meaning, not have this problem, at least).
remove.packages('nimble')
library(devtools)
install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
library(nimble)

(2) Copy the older version of the "RW_llFunction_block" function from the version 0.9.1 version of nimble, available here:
https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/v0.9.1/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R

(3) Or, just define the "extractControlElement" function locally, the code for the (current) version of it is below:

extractControlElement <- function(controlList, elementName, defaultValue, error) {
    if(missing(controlList) | !is.list(controlList))      stop('extractControlElement: controlList argument must be a list')
    if(missing(elementName) | !is.character(elementName)) stop('extractControlElement: elementName argument must be a character string variable name')
    if(missing(defaultValue) & missing(error))            stop('extractControlElement: must provide either defaultValue or error argument')
    if(elementName %in% names(controlList)) {
        return(controlList[[elementName]])
    } else {
        if(!missing(defaultValue)) return(defaultValue) else stop(error)
    }
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

Thank
you for your prompt response, and apologies for this delayed one. It’s been a
chaotic time. We have spent this past few weeks attempting to both investigate the initial values by inspecting (and working with) the model object and determine the cause of
the quartile error.

We followed
both the nimble manual and provided examples, and have worked through some of inappropriate
initialisation values that were present in our model. Additionally, we specified the original model further, and improved certain aspects (I can
provide the updated code for anyone interested). With help from another colleague,
we determined that it was not the original initial values causing the quartile error-
runMCMC() works fine if we do not specify the model to monitor the “X” node.

Without
this monitor the model runs to completion, and the monitored parameters converge. Unfortunately,
it fails to provide a WAIC value, indicating that further latent states need to
be monitored. The same model run on another set of data does not produce this
error. We are currently investigating this issue further and will update once again
we have figured out why, despite setting MCMCmonitorAllSampledNodes=T, WAIC is
being produced as NULL.

This thread has been incredibly helpful in this regard:

https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/issues/799

Again, thank you so much for your time.

Regards,
Zoe Woodgate

On Thursday, August 27, 2020 at 11:38:50 PM UTC+2 pdevalpine wrote:
>
> Hi Zoe,
>
> Thanks for your message.
>
> Let me give a quick answer by pointing you towards some similar issues that have come up on the list:
>
> https://groups.google.com/u/3/g/nimble-users/c/ZZIn3gzKKuY
>
> https://groups.google.com/u/3/g/nimble-users/c/9PmFGuJCrbg
>
> Those illustrate how you can use the model object to inspect variables, log probabilities of stochastic nodes, and control calculations to isolate where something may not be fully initialized.
>
> I am thinking it may be helpful for us to put some easy-to-find guidance up on how to inspect model objects to track down issues like this, maybe as a new example on the web site.  My impression is that perhaps users jumping over from other tools aren't easily seeing what can be done, but let me know how others see it.
>
> Good luck and please let us know if those pointers aren't enough to get you going.
>
> -Perry
>
> On Thu, Aug 27, 2020 at 3:07 AM Zoe Woodgate <woodg...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Good morning everyone,
> >
> > My colleague, Michelle Pretorius <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/ZZIn3gzKKuY/m/Rws9HnvyBQAJ>, recently introduced me to nimble, and like her I am eager to explore its applications (previously I have used STAN to run my multi-spp occu models). Following in her footsteps, we have been trying to run a multi-species, single season occupancy model from Ponisio et al. 2020 <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.6053>, whilst adding in parameters to estimate species richness, similar to Zipkin et al. 2010 <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006320709004819?via%3Dihub>. To do so we are utilising camera trapping data from 3 sites, namely A, B and C. The data does exhibit overdispersion, and I have posted the full code below.
> >
> > However, while running the model we have been getting a fatal error:
> > |-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
> > |-------------------------------------------------------|
> > Error in quantile.default(x, 0.025) :
> >   missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE
> > We suspect that this error is a result of poor model initialization, yet unfortunately we are unsure as to how to troubleshoot this. We have amended the code to not skip over NA records within the input count data in the observation model, as Andrew previously suggested <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/LFEQ4sBUItY>, however this does not appear to have had any impact. In addition, we have noticed that using the direct run() function as opposed to runMCMC() appears to negate this error- but are struggling to understand why. As I understand it, runMCMC allows one to specifiy more arguments and it extracts the samples for you, whilst run() does not. Again, I believe this points to bad model initialisation.
> >
> > In addition, we get multiple warnings. We unsderstand that these can be overlooked:
> > warning: problem initializing stochastic node Z[10, 57]: logProb is -Inf.
> > warning: problem initializing stochastic node Z[12, 57]: logProb is -Inf.
> > ... etc...
> >
> > warning: problem initializing stochastic node X[409, 6, 18]: logProb is -Inf.
> > warning: problem initializing stochastic node X[409, 10, 18]: logProb is -Inf.
> > ... etc...
> > Any assistance/suggestions would be greatly appreciated.
> > Regards,
> > Zoe Woodgate
> > ###########################################################################################
> > # INTIAL DATA PREP
> > ###########################################################################################
> >
> > # Load data
> > survey.data <- read_delim("obs_dates.csv", delim = ",")
> > survey.dates <- read_delim("point_dates.csv", delim = ",")
> > survey.cov <- read_delim( "habitat.csv", delim = ";")
> >
> > # remove duplicate rows in dates column
> > # based on point column
> > survey.dates  <- survey.dates [!duplicated(survey.dates $point), ]
> >
> > # add in random species that covers the stations with zero detections
> > # 12 stations had zero detections
> > point <- c(145, 154, 156, 161, 174, 190, 193, 194, 202, 203, 229, 273)
> > date <- rep(NA, 12)
> > time <- rep(NA, 12)
> > species <- rep("random", 12)
> > individuals <- rep(1,12)
> > repetition <- c(11, 10, 10, 11, 11, 11, 10, 10, 10, 10, 11, 11)
> >
> > # Make new data frame for these missing stations/points
> > missing.data <- data.frame(point, date, time, species, individuals, repetition)
> >
> > #Now add them to original data file
> > survey.data <- rbind(survey.data,missing.data)
> >
> > sort(unique(survey.data$species))
> > # random species is "species 36"
> >
> > ###########################################################################################
> > # HISTORIES (following Ponisio et al. 2020)
> > ###########################################################################################
> >
> > # Use function to create multiple histories for each species per site
> > histories <- createEncounterHistory(survey.data)
> > histories <- addMissingData(histories, survey.dates)
> >
> > histories$X <- histories$X[,,-36] #remove random species
> >
> > # Check random species is removed
> > dim.names <- dimnames(histories$X)
> >
> > X <- histories$X
> >
> > # nzeroes is the number of all zero encounter histories to be added
> > # Augments the original dataset
> > n.zeroes = 10
> >
> > X.aug <- zeroAugment(histories, n.zeroes)
> >
> > ###########################################################################################
> > # PREP DATA FOR MODEL
> > ###########################################################################################
> >
> > # Pull out the number of unique points, species and # reps per station
> > num.species <- length(unique(dim.names[[3]]))
> > num.points <- length(unique(survey.data$point))
> > num.reps <- apply(survey.dates[,-(1:1)],
> >                   1,
> >                   function(x) length(which(!is.na <http://is.na>(x))))
> >
> > # Create a vector to indicate which 'site' (called habitat for ease) type each point is in
> > # For each site, each camera =1, then other site = 0
> > # Repeat for all three sites
> > N <- rep(0, 451)
> > A.id <- c(rep(1, 119), rep(0, (451-119)))
> > B.id <- c(rep(0, 119), rep(1, 176), rep(0, (451-(119+176))))
> > C.id <- c(rep(0, 295), rep(1, (451-295)))
> >
> > ## Standardize variables
> > mpr <- as.numeric(factor(survey.cov$mpr))
> >
> > tri <-  siteLevelStandardized(survey.cov$tri)
> > tri.linear <- tri$linear
> >
> > msavi <- siteLevelStandardized(survey.cov$msavi)
> > msavi.linear <- msavi$linear
> >
> > trail <- siteLevelStandardized(survey.cov$trail)
> > trail <- trail$linear
> >
> > date <- surveyLevelStandardized(survey.dates[,-(1:1)])
> > date.linear <- date$linear
> >
> > # NA's -> 0's
> > date.linear[is.na <http://is.na>(date.linear)] <- 0
> >
> > # Z data for whether or not a species was ever observed
> > # zs with 1s as 1s and 0s as NAs
> > class(X.aug)
> > zs <- apply(X.aug, c(1, 3), max, na.rm=TRUE)
> > zs[zs == 0] <- NA
> > zs[!is.finite(zs)] <- NA
> >
> > model.data <- list(Z = zs,
> >                    X = X.aug,
> >                    mpr=mpr,
> >                    A.id=A.id,
> >                    B.id=B.id,
> >                    C.id=C.id,
> >                    tri.linear=tri.linear,
> >                    msavi.linear=msavi.linear,
> >                    trail=trail,
> >                    date.linear = date.linear)
> >
> > psi.mean.draw <- runif(1, 0.25, 1)
> >
> > # initial values
> >
> > omega.draw <- runif(1, num.species/(num.species + n.zeroes), 1)
> >
> > # initial conditions. 1 should be NA, NA should be a 0 or 1
> > zinits <- zs
> > zinits[zinits == 1] <- 2
> > zinits[is.na <http://is.na>(zinits)] <- sample(0:1, sum(is.na <http://is.na>(zinits)),
> >                                 replace=TRUE)
> > zinits[zinits == 2] <- NA
> >
> > # Make list of intial value data for model to call upon
> >
> > initsList <-list(Z=zinits,
> >                  omega = omega.draw,
> >                  w = c(rep(1, num.species),
> >                        rbinom(n.zeroes, size = 1, prob = omega.draw)),
> >                  u.A = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  v.A = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  u.B = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes) ,
> >                  v.B = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  u.C = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes) ,
> >                  v.C = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  a1 = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  a2 = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  a3 = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  b1 = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes),
> >                  b2 = rnorm(num.species + n.zeroes))
> >
> > # Further information needed for the model
> > constants <- list(num.species = num.species,
> >                   num.points = num.points,
> >                   num.reps = num.reps,
> >                   n.zeroes = n.zeroes)
> >
> > ################################################################################
> > # BUGS CODE WITH NIMBLE
> > ################################################################################
> >
> > # Construct the initial values
> > ms.ss.occ <- nimbleCode({
> >   ## Define prior distributions for community-level model parameters
> >
> >   omega ~ dunif(0,1)
> >
> >   A.occ.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.uA <- log(A.occ.mean) - log(1-A.occ.mean)
> >   sigma.uA ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.uA <-  1/(sigma.uA*sigma.uA)
> >
> >   B.occ.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.uB <- log(B.occ.mean) - log(1-B.occ.mean)
> >   sigma.uB ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.uB <-  1/(sigma.uB*sigma.uB)
> >
> >   C.occ.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.uC <- log(C.occ.mean) - log(1-C.occ.mean)
> >   sigma.uC ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.uC <-  1/(sigma.uC*sigma.uC)
> >
> >   A.det.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.vA <- log(A.det.mean) - log(1-A.det.mean)
> >   sigma.vA ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.vA <-  1/(sigma.vA*sigma.vA)
> >
> >   B.det.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.vB <- log(B.det.mean) - log(1-B.det.mean)
> >   sigma.vB ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.vB <-  1/(sigma.vB*sigma.vB)
> >
> >   C.det.mean ~ dunif(0,1)
> >   mu.vC <- log(C.det.mean) - log(1-C.det.mean)
> >   sigma.vC ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.vC <-  1/(sigma.vC*sigma.vC)
> >
> >   ## random effects
> >   mu.a1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
> >   sigma.a1 ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.a1 <-  1/(sigma.a1*sigma.a1)
> >
> >   mu.a2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
> >   sigma.a2 ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.a2 <-  1/(sigma.a2*sigma.a2)
> >
> >   mu.a3 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
> >   sigma.a3 ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.a3 <-  1/(sigma.a3*sigma.a3)
> >
> >   mu.b1 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
> >   sigma.b1 ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.b1 <-  1/(sigma.b1*sigma.b1)
> >
> >   mu.b2 ~ dnorm(0, 0.001)
> >   sigma.b2 ~ dunif(0, 100)
> >   tau.b2 <-  1/(sigma.b2*sigma.b2)
> >
> >   for (i in 1:(num.species + n.zeroes)) {
> >     ## Create priors for species i from the community level prior distributions
> >
> >     w[i] ~ dbern(omega)
> >
> >     u.A[i] ~ dnorm(mu.uA, tau.uA)
> >     u.B[i] ~ dnorm(mu.uB, tau.uB)
> >     u.C[i] ~ dnorm(mu.uC, tau.uC)
> >
> >     a1[i] ~ dnorm(mu.a1, tau.a1)
> >     a2[i] ~ dnorm(mu.a2, tau.a2)
> >     a3[i] ~ dnorm(mu.a3, tau.a3)
> >
> >     v.A[i] ~ dnorm(mu.vA, tau.vA)
> >     v.B[i] ~ dnorm(mu.vB, tau.vB)
> >     v.C[i] ~ dnorm(mu.vC, tau.vC)
> >
> >     b1[i] ~ dnorm(mu.b1, tau.b1)
> >     b2[i] ~ dnorm(mu.b2, tau.b2)
> >
> >     ## Create a loop to estimate the Z matrix (true occurrence for species i at point j).
> >
> >     ## A=2; B=1; C=0
> >
> >     for (j in 1:num.points) {
> >       logit(psi[j,i]) <- u.A[i]*A.id[j] +
> >         u.B[i]*B.id[j] +
> >         u.C[i]*C.id[j] +
> >         a1[i]*mpr[j] +
> >         a2[i]*tri.linear[j] +
> >         a3[i]*msavi.linear[j]
> >
> >       mu.psi[j,i] <- psi[j,i]*w[i]
> >       Z[j,i] ~ dbern(mu.psi[j,i])
> >
> >       ## Create a loop to estimate detection for species i at point k during sampling period k.
> >
> >       for (k in 1:max(num.reps[j])) {
> >         logit(p[j,k,i]) <-  v.A[i]*A.id[j] +
> >           v.B[i]*B.id[j] +
> >           v.C[i]*C.id[j] +
> >           b1[i]*trail[j]+
> >           b2[i]*date.linear[j,k]
> >
> >         mu.p[j,k,i] <- p[j,k,i]*Z[j,i]
> >         X[j,k,i] ~ dbern(mu.p[j,k,i])
> >       }
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   ## Sum all species observed (n) and unobserved species (n0) to find the total estimated richness
> >
> >   n0 <- sum(w[(num.species+1):(num.species+n.zeroes)])
> >   N <- num.species + n0
> >
> >   ## Create a loop to determine point level richness estimates for the whole community and for subsets or assemblages of interest.
> >
> >   for(j in 1:num.points){
> >     Nsite[j]<- inprod(Z[j,1:(num.species+n.zeroes)],w[1:(num.species+n.zeroes)])
> >   }
> > })
> >
> > ###########################################################################################
> > # NIMBLE MODEL
> > ###########################################################################################
> >
> > Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code=ms.ss.occ,
> >                       data=model.data,
> >                       inits = initsList,
> >                       constants=constants)
> >
> > nimbleOptions(MCMCuseSamplerAssignmentRules = TRUE)
> >
> > customSpec <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, condition = quote({
> >
> >   ## *********************************************************************
> >   ##  block sampler for species random effects for each species, RW
> >   ## *********************************************************************
> >
> >   customSpec <- configureMCMC(Rmodel)
> >   sigma.nodes <-  Rmodel$getNodeNames(stochOnly=TRUE)[grepl("sigma",
